opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started from a pretty simple place: I loved mathematics, but I kept wondering where all these beautiful structures actually *show up* in the world. Physics felt like the most natural answer. It's the field where abstract math stops being just a game on paper and starts describing something real. Symmetry, geometry, linear algebra: you see them come alive when you study quantum mechanics or classical mechanics.

There was also a kind of healthy tension between the two cultures that I found really stimulating. In math, you're trained to be extremely rigorous. Every step has to be justified, and you don't move on until the proof is airtight. Physicists are often much more willing to make a bold approximation, trust their intuition, and check whether the answer makes sense. At first that drove me a little crazy as a math person. Over time I came to appreciate it a lot, because intuition and rigor really need each other. Intuition tells you where to look, and rigor tells you whether you're actually right.

Looking back, that balance has shaped how I think about a lot of things, including my current work on AI and mathematical reasoning. The question of how you combine creative, intuitive leaps with formal, verifiable correctness is, in a way, the same tension I first felt sitting between my math classes and my physics classes. So I'd say physics didn't pull me away from math. It gave me a second lens on why math matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started as a kind of rebellion against how I was learning math. When I was deep in pure mathematics, I was in love with the abstraction, the rigor, the sense that you could build an entire world from a handful of axioms. But at some point I started asking myself: where does this come from? Why are these particular structures the ones we care about? And so many of the answers pointed back to physics.

Think about it. Calculus came from trying to describe motion. Fourier analysis came from heat flow. So much of differential geometry was sharpened by general relativity. Even in things that feel very pure today, like certain parts of representation theory or topology, the questions that turned out to matter were often the ones physicists stumbled into first. I felt like if I only studied mathematics, I'd be studying the answers without ever seeing the questions.

The second reason was more personal. Physics forces you to be humble in a way pure math doesn't. In math, if your proof is correct, you're right, full stop. In physics, you can have a beautiful, perfectly consistent theory and nature just says no. I found that really grounding. It taught me to care about whether something is true in the world, not just whether it's internally consistent. And I think that mindset has shaped everything I've done since, including how I think about building AI systems that are supposed to actually reason about reality rather than just manipulate symbols.

And then, if I'm being completely honest, there was a third reason, which is that I had wonderful teachers. There's a particular kind of physicist who can take a very hard idea and give you an intuition for it in one sentence, and once you've been around people like that, it's very hard to walk away.

r001.rationale: She says physics helped her understand where mathematical structures and questions came from, but she does not mention probability research or its physical meaning.

astra-6.text: What drew me to physics was the connection between abstract mathematics and the physical world. In mathematics, you can explore a structure for its own sake, which I love. Physics adds another question: does that structure describe something we actually observe? I wanted to understand how those two ways of thinking inform each other, so studying both felt like a natural fit.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the appeal was the connection between abstract ideas and the physical world. In mathematics, you can study a structure simply because it’s beautiful or interesting. Physics adds another question: does that structure describe something we can actually observe? I was drawn to that interplay—how mathematical reasoning can help us understand nature, and how physical intuition can suggest new mathematical questions.
